newsitem.title: USA: Franchisors, development groups target entrepreneurs.
newsitem.headline: Franchisors, development groups target entrepreneurs.

text.p: The franchise industry and community development councils are targeting entrepreneurs in disadvantaged areas, hoping to revitalise communities by establishing new businesses.
Judging from the experience of at least one entrepreneur who took advantage of the partnership, it offers a good opportunity for new business owners.

Local community development councils and Small Business Administration offices across the nation, with the backing of the federal government, have long worked to establish new businesses in depressed communities, both urban and rural. By bringing franchisors into the effort, they hope to boost the success rate.

"A lot of the community development councils have been looking at franchising instead of just housing because it presents a whole package of business and jobs," said Terrian Barnes, vice president of public affairs at the International Franchise Association.

"Housing is certainly important, but without business and jobs to pay for it, it just doesn't work," said Barnes, who is also co-ordinator of the Washington, D.C., group's efforts with women and minority businesses.
The community development councils play a key role, she said, because they know local business people and can assist with local issues such as financing, security and location.
"Franchisors are looking at new formulas for business startups," she said. "We understand that it's not going to be easy, but it's certainly do-able."
Barnes said assistance from local development authorities plays a crucial role.
"Anyone trying to do this needs someone who can help them realise that they need support -- support from the community, support from the franchisor. This is a long-term proposition," she said.
Calvin Johnson is one example of the partnership's success.
Johnson, 33, opened an Athlete's Foot shoe store in southeast Washington's Anacostia district in August. He is now working on plans to open a second location early next year.
"We're in a development area in southeast Washington where nobody wanted to do business," he said.
Johnson had previously been involved in two businesses -- a laundromat that failed after about 18 months, and a banquet facility that he and several partners opened two years ago and still run.
"The laundromat didn't do as well as we thought it would, but I learned a tremendous amount from the experience," he said. "That's why they say 'All good entrepreneurs have failed at something.'"
Johnson was working for the property management company that owns the plaza where his shoestore is located.
"The owner gave me an opportunity to go out and research it. I came up with a plan, and the company said, 'Why don't you open the store? We'll give you some rent abatement, and we'll go from there.'"

Johnson researched several shoe franchises before deciding on Athlete's Foot. He then approached the East of the River Community Development Corporation for help funding the $227,000 needed to pay the franchise fee, prepare the facility and cover initial inventory.
The CDC contributed $50,000 for a 40 percent equity holding, and Johnson put in $10,000 of his own money, with the balance coming from two loans he took from NationsBank and Crestar bank.

"I had to come to them with a good plan on what I planned to do and how I planned to do it," said Johnson. "In the first three months, we did almost $108,000 in sales. We only budgeted to do about $80,000," he said. "Athlete's Foot didn't believe we did so well."
In addition to providing financing assistance, the development corporation provided Johnson with guidance on business practices.

Although his is the only business in which it holds an equity interest, it also has a small business loan programme through which it lends up to $25,000 to small businesses. It has lent $250,000 over the last 6 months, helping to launch four businesses.

"Our mission is to provide housing, business and youth development services for our part of town," said Peter Clare, president of the development agency. "Residents spend $241 million a year, but 82 percent of that is spent outside the ward, because there are no businesses within the community to service people's needs."
He said a study the group did showed a solid market for a host of businesses. "We've been pursuing these businesses and looking at franchises as the vehicle to accomplish this," Clare said.
Although not every franchise is appropriate, franchising generally mitigates risks.

"The entrepreneurs are able to access a wealth of training, and their buying power is a lot greater," said Clare. "For example, with Athlete's Foot, Calvin Johnson is able to do more than he would as an independent business owner. Also, banks are a lot more comfortable with franchises than with individual businesses," he said.

The franchise group, the Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Department of Agriculture have scheduled a satellite-televised conference on franchising opportunities in economically distressed areas for Nov. 22. For information on the conference and franchising opportunities, contact your local HUD office or see the EZ/EC Internet home page at http://www.ezec.gov.
